title: Intake vacuum leak smoke test
text: Applies to all gasoline engines. With the engine off, introduce smoke into the intake through the brake booster vacuum line and watch the intake manifold gasket, throttle body gasket, PCV hoses and vacuum lines for escaping smoke. A lean code that is worst at idle and improves above 2,000 rpm usually indicates unmetered air entering after the airflow sensor.
step: With the engine off, smoke-test the intake through the brake booster vacuum line and watch the manifold gasket, throttle body gasket, PCV hoses and vacuum lines for escaping smoke
results: A shop smoke-tested the intake for me. No smoke came out anywhere.
The smoke test was clean, nothing leaking at the manifold, throttle body or hoses.

title: Fuel pressure and hold test, returnless systems
text: Applies to all gasoline engines with a fuel rail test port. Key on, engine off, connect a pressure gauge at the rail test port. Specified pressure is 55-62 psi, and it should hold within 5 psi for 5 minutes after key-off. Low pressure can produce lean codes and a rough idle; low pressure together with high fuel trims at all speeds points to fuel delivery.
step: Key on, engine off, connect a gauge at the fuel rail test port and confirm 55-62 psi that holds within 5 psi for 5 minutes after key-off
results: Borrowed a gauge. It read 58 psi and held for the full five minutes.
Fuel pressure was 60 psi key on and barely dropped after I shut it off.

title: Mass airflow sensor reading at idle
text: Applies to all gasoline engines with a mass airflow sensor. With the engine at operating temperature and idling with all accessories off, read MAF airflow on a scan tool. Expect roughly 1 g/s per liter of displacement (about 2-2.5 g/s for a 2.0L engine). A reading well below that while long-term fuel trim is high suggests the sensor is under-reporting airflow.
step: With the engine warm and idling and the accessories off, read mass airflow on a scan tool and compare it with roughly 1 g/s per liter of displacement
results: The scan tool shows the MAF right about where it should be for my engine size at idle.
MAF reading at warm idle matched the 1 g/s per liter rule almost exactly.

title: Residual fuel pressure after hot shutdown
text: Applies to all gasoline engines with a fuel rail test port. Drive until the engine is at full operating temperature, shut it off with a gauge on the rail test port and record the pressure 20 minutes later. Pressure should stay above 30 psi. A faster drop lets fuel boil in the hot rail, which shows up as a long crank on restarts after a short stop.
step: Drive until the engine is fully warm, shut it off with a gauge on the fuel rail test port and read the pressure 20 minutes later; it should still be above 30 psi
results: Put a gauge on after a drive. Still 42 psi after twenty minutes.
Residual pressure held at about 40 psi twenty minutes after shutdown.

title: Coolant temperature sensor plausibility check
text: Applies to all engines. With the engine fully warm, compare the engine coolant temperature (ECT) reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading taken at the thermostat housing. The two should agree within 10 deg F. A sensor that reads cold on a hot engine makes the control module add extra fuel on restart, which can flood a hot engine.
step: With the engine fully warm, compare the coolant temperature reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading at the thermostat housing; they should agree within 10 deg F
results: Scan tool said 201 and the infrared gun said 196 at the housing.
Coolant temp on the scanner and the IR reading were within a few degrees of each other.

title: Clear-flood crank test for hot restart concerns
text: Applies to all gasoline engines. On a hot restart, crank with the accelerator pedal held to the floor; the control module cuts injector pulse in this clear-flood mode. If the engine starts noticeably faster in clear-flood mode, it is being overfueled on hot restarts. If it cranks just as long, excess fuel is unlikely and fuel supply or spark should be examined.
step: On a hot restart, crank with the accelerator held to the floor to put the engine in clear-flood mode and note whether it fires noticeably faster
results: Tried it with the pedal floored on a hot restart. Cranked just as long, no difference.
The clear-flood trick made no difference. Still a long crank when it's hot.

title: Slow cranking on a hot engine
text: Applies to all vehicles. If the engine turns over noticeably slower when hot than when cold, measure starter current draw with an inductive clamp while cranking with fuel disabled. Draw above 250 A on a four- or six-cylinder engine indicates excessive starter load. This procedure covers slow crank speed only, not an engine that cranks at normal speed but is slow to fire.

title: Spark output test with an adjustable spark tester
text: Applies to all engines with individual coil-on-plug ignition. Remove the coil from the misfiring cylinder, connect an adjustable spark tester set to 25 kV between the coil and engine ground, and crank with fuel disabled. A strong blue spark should jump the gap on every crank. A weak, orange or intermittent spark indicates the coil cannot supply enough voltage under load.
step: Connect an adjustable spark tester set to 25 kV to the coil from the misfiring cylinder and crank with fuel disabled, watching for a strong blue spark on every crank
results: Hooked up a spark tester at 25 kV. Strong blue spark every time.
The spark tester showed a solid blue spark the whole time I cranked it.

title: Spark plug inspection and gap check
text: Applies to all gasoline engines. Remove the spark plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with a plug from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in) and look for a cracked insulator, carbon tracking down the porcelain, or oil or fuel fouling.
step: Pull the spark plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with one from a good cylinder, checking the gap and looking for a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or fouling
results: Pulled the plug. Gap is 0.042, no cracks, and it looks like the others.
The plug from that cylinder looks clean and is gapped right, no tracking on the porcelain.

title: Cranking compression test
text: Applies to all gasoline engines. Disable fuel and ignition, remove all spark plugs and crank each cylinder through at least five compression strokes with the throttle held open. All cylinders should read within 10 percent of each other. A cylinder that reads low points to a mechanical cause rather than an ignition or fuel cause.
step: With fuel and ignition disabled and the throttle held open, run a cranking compression test and compare the misfiring cylinder with the rest
results: Compression was 175 to 180 on every cylinder, including the one with the code.
All cylinders came in within a few psi of each other on compression.

title: Electric radiator fan operation check
text: Applies to vehicles with electric radiator fans (2.0L I4, 2.4L I4, 2.5L I4, 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 1.4L turbo I4, 3.5L V6 and 3.4L V6 engines; not the 5.5L V8). With the engine at operating temperature and idling, turn the AC on or command the radiator fan on with a scan tool. The fan should start within a few moments. A fan that does not run lets coolant temperature climb in traffic while highway airflow keeps it normal at speed.
step: With the engine warm and idling, turn the AC on or command the radiator fan on with a scan tool and confirm the fan starts
results: Turned the AC on and the radiator fan kicked on right away.
Commanded the fan with my scanner and it spun up on both speeds.

title: Coolant level and trapped air check
text: Applies to all engines. With the engine cold, remove the radiator cap or degas bottle cap and check that coolant is at the neck or the cold-fill line. Low coolant, or air trapped near the thermostat housing, causes temperature to swing upward at idle while airflow at speed can mask it.
step: With the engine cold, open the radiator or degas bottle cap and look at whether coolant is right up to the neck or the cold-fill line
results: Checked it cold this morning. Coolant is right up to the neck.
Level is at the cold-fill line, nothing low.

title: Radiator temperature drop check
text: Applies to all engines. With the engine at operating temperature and the thermostat open, use an infrared thermometer to compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank. A drop of 20-40 deg F is typical. A much smaller drop, or cold spots across the core, indicates restricted flow through the radiator.
step: With the engine at operating temperature, compare the radiator inlet and outlet tank temperatures with an infrared thermometer and scan the core for cold spots
results: Inlet was 205 and outlet 172, and I didn't find any cold spots on the core.
About a 30 degree drop across the radiator and an even temperature across the core.

title: Cooling system pressure test
text: Applies to all engines. With the engine cold, fit a cooling system pressure tester to the radiator neck or reservoir and pump to the pressure stamped on the cap. Pressure should hold for 15 minutes. While the system is pressurized, inspect the hoses, the heater hoses at the firewall, the water pump weep hole and the radiator end tanks for seepage.
step: With the engine cold, pressurize the cooling system to the cap rating and watch for a pressure drop over 15 minutes while you inspect the hoses, water pump weep hole and radiator tanks
results: Pressure-tested it cold. Held steady for 15 minutes and nothing dripped.
It held 16 psi for fifteen minutes with no wet spots anywhere.

title: Pressure cap test
text: Applies to all engines. Fit the radiator or reservoir cap to a cap adapter on the pressure tester and pump until the cap vents. It should hold at least its stamped rating. A cap that vents early lets coolant escape through the overflow as vapor, which can lower the level with no visible leak or puddle.
step: Test the radiator or reservoir cap on a cap adapter and confirm it holds at least its stamped pressure rating
results: The cap held its rated 16 psi on the adapter.
Tested the cap and it didn't vent until past its rating.

title: Combustion leak (block) test
text: Applies to all engines. With the engine warm and idling, remove the reservoir cap and use a combustion leak tester to draw air from above the coolant through the test fluid. Blue fluid that turns yellow or green indicates combustion gases in the coolant. Keep the test fluid out of the coolant itself.
step: With the engine warm and idling, run a combustion leak test by drawing air from above the coolant through the tester fluid and watching for a color change
results: Ran the block tester. The fluid stayed blue the whole time.
Combustion leak test showed no color change at all.

title: Thermostat opening check
text: Applies to all engines. From a cold start, idle the engine and watch coolant temperature on a scan tool while feeling the upper radiator hose. The hose should stay cool until about 195 deg F and warm quickly after that. An engine that takes more than 15 minutes to reach 190 deg F, or an upper hose that warms early, indicates a thermostat that is stuck open.
step: From a cold start, watch coolant temperature on a scan tool while feeling the upper radiator hose; it should stay cool until about 195 deg F
results: The upper hose stayed cool until the scanner showed about 196, and it got hot fast after that.
Reached 195 in about eight minutes and the upper hose warmed right at that point.

title: Heater core inlet and outlet temperature check
text: Applies to all engines. With the engine at operating temperature, the heat set to full hot and the blower on high, measure both heater hoses at the firewall with an infrared thermometer. Both hoses should be hot and within about 15 deg F of each other. A cool outlet hose with a hot inlet indicates restricted flow through the heater core.
step: With the engine at operating temperature and the heat on full, measure both heater hoses at the firewall with an infrared thermometer and compare them
results: Both heater hoses are hot, 182 and 174.
Inlet and outlet heater hoses were within about ten degrees, both hot to the touch.

title: Blend door actuator travel check
text: Applies to all models. With the engine warm, run the climate control from full cold to full hot while listening behind the center of the dash. The blend door actuator should move smoothly through its full travel without clicking or stopping short. On systems with a self-test, the actuator sweeps full travel at the start of the test.
step: With the engine warm, sweep the temperature control from full cold to full hot and listen behind the center of the dash for the blend door actuator moving through its full travel
results: I can hear the door move all the way across and it doesn't click or stop.
The actuator sweeps smoothly from cold to hot, no clicking.

title: Coolant level check for low heater output
text: Applies to all engines. In many cooling systems the heater core sits at the highest point, so it is the first part of the system to lose flow when coolant is low. With the engine cold, check the level at the radiator neck or degas bottle rather than relying on the overflow tank mark.
step: With the engine cold, check the coolant level at the radiator neck or degas bottle rather than the overflow tank
results: Coolant is full at the radiator neck.
Checked at the degas bottle cold and it's right at the line.

title: Parasitic draw test
text: Applies to all vehicles. Close the doors, latch the hood switch closed and let the modules go to sleep, which can take up to 45 minutes. Connect an ammeter in series at the negative battery terminal without breaking the circuit. Draw should settle below 50 mA. A higher draw indicates a circuit that stays awake.
step: With the doors closed and the modules asleep, connect an ammeter in series at the negative battery terminal; draw should settle below 50 mA
results: Waited 45 minutes and the draw settled at 28 mA.
Meter read 0.03 amps once everything went to sleep.

title: Battery state-of-health test
text: Applies to all vehicles. Fully charge the battery and let it rest for at least one hour. Resting voltage should be 12.6 V or higher. Run a conductance or load test and compare the result with the cold cranking amps (CCA) rating on the label. A battery below about 70 percent of its rating cannot hold enough charge to survive several days parked.
step: Fully charge the battery, let it rest, and run a conductance or load test against the CCA rating on its label
results: Charged it overnight and the tester says 680 CCA against a 700 rating. It passed.
Resting voltage was 12.7 and it passed the load test.

title: Recharge check for repeat dead batteries
text: Applies to all vehicles. A battery that is not brought back to full charge during normal driving goes flat after a few days parked even with no excess draw. After a 20 minute drive, with the engine at 2,000 rpm and the headlights and blower on, measure voltage at the battery posts. A reading of 13.5-14.7 V shows the charging system is recharging the battery.
step: After a 20 minute drive, with the engine at 2,000 rpm and the headlights and blower on, measure voltage at the battery posts and compare it with 13.5-14.7 V
results: After the drive it showed 14.2 V at the battery with the lights and blower on.
Charging voltage was 13.9 volts at 2,000 rpm.

title: Charging voltage test under load
text: Applies to all vehicles. With the engine at 2,000 rpm and the headlights, blower on high and rear defrost on, measure voltage across the battery posts. Expect 13.5-14.7 V. A reading below 13.0 V with loads on indicates low charging output.
step: With the engine at 2,000 rpm and the headlights, blower and rear defrost on, measure voltage across the battery posts and compare it with 13.5-14.7 V
results: 14.1 volts at the battery with everything on.
The meter showed 13.9 V at 2,000 rpm with all the loads on.

title: Accessory drive belt and tensioner inspection
text: Applies to all vehicles with a belt-driven alternator. With the engine off, inspect the accessory drive belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs, and confirm the tensioner indicator sits within its marked range. A glazed belt or weak tensioner lets the alternator pulley slip at idle under electrical load.
step: With the engine off, inspect the accessory belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs and confirm the tensioner indicator is within its marked range
results: The belt looks new, no glazing, and the tensioner mark is in the middle of the range.
Belt and tensioner both look fine, no cracks.

title: Alternator AC ripple test
text: Applies to all vehicles. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Higher ripple indicates a failed diode in the alternator rectifier, which reduces output and can cause lights to flicker.
step: With the engine at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, measure AC ripple voltage across the battery posts and compare it with 0.5 V AC
results: Ripple was 0.08 volts AC.
AC ripple measured well under half a volt.

title: Charging circuit voltage drop test
text: Applies to all vehicles. With the engine at 2,000 rpm and heavy electrical loads on, measure voltage drop from the alternator output terminal to the battery positive post, and from the alternator case to the battery negative post. Drop should be under 0.3 V on the positive side and under 0.2 V on the ground side.
step: With the engine at 2,000 rpm and heavy loads on, measure voltage drop between the alternator output terminal and the battery positive post
results: 0.1 V drop on the positive side and 0.05 on the ground side.
Voltage drop across the charging cables was tiny, under a tenth of a volt.

title: Starter circuit voltage drop test
text: Applies to all vehicles. With a helper holding the ignition in the start position, measure voltage drop from the battery positive post to the starter B+ terminal, and from the battery negative post to the engine block. Each side should be under 0.5 V. A higher drop means the starter cannot draw enough current to turn the engine, even when the battery is charged.
step: With a helper holding the key in start, measure voltage drop from the battery positive post to the starter B+ terminal; it should be under 0.5 V
results: Positive side drop was 0.2 V while it clicked.
Measured 0.3 volts on the positive cable during the start attempt.

title: Battery voltage during a start attempt
text: Applies to all vehicles. Connect a meter across the battery posts and watch the reading while a helper attempts to start the engine. Voltage should not fall below 9.6 V. A battery that collapses below that value cannot power the starter even if dash lights look bright with the key on.
step: Connect a meter across the battery posts and watch the lowest voltage while a helper attempts a start; it should stay above 9.6 V
results: Battery stayed at 12.2 volts when it clicked.
Voltage only dipped to 11.9 on the start attempt.

title: Starter control circuit check
text: Applies to all vehicles. Back-probe the starter solenoid S terminal and have a helper attempt a start in park. The S terminal should receive at least 10.5 V during the attempt. Low or no voltage points to the control side (relay, range switch or wiring) rather than the starter itself.
step: Back-probe the starter solenoid S terminal while a helper attempts a start in park; it should get at least 10.5 V
results: Got 11.8 volts at the S terminal when it clicks.
The S terminal sees about 11.5 V on the start attempt.

title: Rotor lateral runout measurement
text: Applies to all vehicles with front disc brakes. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the steering knuckle and set the plunger about 0.5 in from the outer edge of the rotor face. Rotate the rotor one full turn. Lateral runout must not exceed 0.002 in.
step: With the lug nuts torqued to spec, mount a dial indicator on the knuckle and measure front rotor lateral runout about half an inch in from the edge against the 0.002 in limit
results: Runout on both front rotors was 0.001 inch.
Dial indicator showed under a thousandth on both sides.

title: Rotor thickness variation
text: Applies to all vehicles with front disc brakes. Using an outside micrometer, measure rotor thickness at eight evenly spaced points about 0.5 in from the outer edge. Thickness variation must not exceed 0.0005 in. Variation above this limit produces pedal pulsation during braking from speed.
step: Measure front rotor thickness with a micrometer at eight evenly spaced points about half an inch from the edge; variation should be under 0.0005 in
results: Thickness variation was 0.0003 inch on both rotors.
Micrometer readings varied by less than half a thousandth around each rotor.

title: Rotor surface inspection for uneven pad transfer
text: Applies to all vehicles with front disc brakes. Remove the front wheels and inspect both faces of each rotor in good light. Dark, blotchy patches of pad material, or blue-gray hard spots that a file skates over, indicate uneven pad transfer or hard spots that grab the pad once per revolution and are felt as pulsation when braking from speed.
step: With the front wheels off, inspect both faces of each front rotor in good light for dark patches of pad material or blue-gray hard spots
results: Rotor faces look even all the way around, no dark patches or hard spots.
Both rotors have a uniform finish on both faces, nothing blotchy.

title: Caliper slide pin check
text: Applies to all vehicles with floating front calipers. Remove each front caliper from its bracket without disconnecting the hose. Pull each slide pin from its bore and check for corrosion, swelling of the boot, or binding. Pins should move freely by hand through their full travel. A binding pin causes uneven pad pressure and a pull during braking.
step: Remove the front calipers from their brackets and confirm each slide pin moves freely through its full travel without binding
results: Slide pins on both sides slide freely, no rust.
Pulled the pins on both calipers. Clean and they move fine.

title: Brake hose restriction test
text: Applies to all vehicles. With the front wheels off the ground, have a helper press and release the brake pedal firmly. Immediately spin each front wheel by hand. Both wheels should turn freely right after release. A wheel that stays dragged for several moments indicates a hose that is restricting fluid return.
step: With the front wheels raised, have a helper press and release the brake pedal and spin each front wheel right away to see whether either one stays dragged
results: Both front wheels spin freely right after the pedal is released.
Neither wheel drags after letting off the pedal.

title: Brake temperature comparison
text: Applies to all vehicles. After a test drive with several moderate stops, park without using the parking brake and measure each front rotor face with an infrared thermometer. Temperatures should be within about 50 deg F side to side. A large difference shows which side is braking harder or dragging.
step: After a test drive with several moderate stops, measure both front rotor faces with an infrared thermometer and compare the two sides
results: Left rotor was 212 and the right 205 after the drive.
Both rotors were within about 15 degrees of each other.

title: Front tire match and pressure check
text: Applies to all vehicles. Check that both front tires are the same size, brand, model and approximate tread depth, and set cold pressures to the door placard. A mismatched tire, or a large pressure difference side to side, can cause a pull that is most noticeable under braking.
step: Check that both front tires match in size, brand and tread depth and that cold pressures match the door placard
results: Both fronts are the same brand and size, about the same tread, and 35 psi each.
Tires match side to side and pressures were already on the placard.

title: Stabilizer link inspection
text: Applies to all vehicles with a front stabilizer bar. With the vehicle on the ground so the suspension is loaded, grasp each stabilizer link and push and pull firmly. Watch both ball studs for play or a knock. Any free play, or a torn boot with grease loss, indicates a worn link.
step: With the vehicle on the ground, grasp each front stabilizer link and push and pull firmly while watching both ball studs for play
results: Links are tight, no play at either end.
Both stabilizer links feel solid with no knock.

title: Strut upper mount check
text: Applies to all vehicles with front struts. With a helper bouncing the front of the vehicle, rest a hand on the strut upper mount under the hood and feel for a knock. With the engine running, turn the steering lock to lock and feel for binding or a pop at the mount bearing.
step: With a helper bouncing the front of the vehicle, rest a hand on each strut upper mount under the hood and feel for a knock
results: Couldn't feel any knock at the top mounts while it was bounced.
Strut mounts feel quiet and solid when bouncing the front.

title: Lower ball joint play check
text: Applies to all vehicles. Raise the vehicle with a jack under the lower control arm so the ball joint is loaded. Place a pry bar under the tire and lift while watching the joint between the knuckle and control arm. Specification is zero measurable vertical play.
step: With a jack under the lower control arm, lift the tire with a pry bar and watch the lower ball joint for any vertical play
results: No movement at the lower ball joints with the pry bar.
Pried on both sides and saw zero play at the ball joints.

title: Road-force wheel balance check
text: Applies to all vehicles. Check each wheel and tire assembly on a road-force balancer. Static and dynamic imbalance should be under 0.25 oz, and road-force variation should be under about 20 lb for passenger tires. A vibration that peaks in a narrow band such as 60-70 mph usually comes from the wheel and tire assemblies.
step: Check each wheel and tire on a road-force balancer for imbalance and road-force variation
results: A shop road-force balanced all four and they were all within spec.
Balance was fine on every wheel and the road-force numbers were low.

title: Tire radial runout check
text: Applies to all vehicles. With the vehicle raised, set a dial indicator against the center tread rib and rotate each tire one full turn. Radial runout should not exceed 0.060 in. A higher reading indicates an out-of-round tire or a bent wheel.
step: With the vehicle raised, set a dial indicator on the center tread rib and measure radial runout of each tire against the 0.060 in limit
results: Radial runout was 0.030 inch or less on every tire.
Every tire measured well under the runout limit.

title: Tire tread and belt inspection
text: Applies to all vehicles. With the vehicle raised, slowly rotate each tire and run a gloved hand across the tread and sidewalls. Feel for lumps, a wavy tread line or cupping, which indicate a shifted belt or separation. Look for a tread rib that wanders as the tire turns.
step: With the vehicle raised, rotate each tire slowly and run a gloved hand across the tread and sidewalls feeling for lumps, cupping or a wavy tread line
results: No lumps or cupping on any of them.
Tread runs straight on all four and I didn't feel anything odd.

title: Brake fluid level and leak inspection
text: Applies to all vehicles. Check the master cylinder reservoir level against the MIN and MAX marks. Inspect each caliper, wheel cylinder, brake hose and steel line for wetness, and check the joint between the master cylinder and the brake booster for fluid seepage from the rear seal.
step: Check the reservoir level and inspect each caliper, hose, line and the master cylinder-to-booster joint for fluid wetness
results: Reservoir is at MAX and there are no wet spots at any wheel or at the master cylinder.
Fluid level is fine and everything looks dry.

title: Master cylinder bypass test
text: Applies to all vehicles. With the engine off, pump the brake pedal several times to use up booster reserve. Apply steady, moderate pressure to the pedal and hold it for one minute. A pedal that slowly sinks toward the floor with no external leak indicates fluid bypassing inside the master cylinder.
step: With the engine off and the booster reserve pumped out, hold steady moderate pressure on the pedal for one minute and watch whether it slowly sinks
results: Held it for a full minute with the engine off and the pedal didn't sink.
Pedal stayed put under steady pressure for the whole minute.

title: Brake fluid moisture test
text: Applies to all vehicles. Test the fluid in the reservoir with a brake fluid tester or test strip. Fluid with more than 3 percent water has a reduced boiling point and can vaporize in the calipers, producing a soft pedal. Fluid that is dark or cloudy also indicates contamination.
step: Test the fluid in the reservoir with a brake fluid tester or test strip and compare its water content with the 3 percent limit
results: The tester shows about 1 percent moisture.
Test strip came back in the good range, fluid looks clear.

title: Compressor clutch engagement check
text: Applies to all models with a clutch-driven compressor. With the engine running, the AC at maximum and the blower on high, watch the compressor front plate. The plate should pull in and spin with the pulley. A plate that stays still, or cycles on and off every few moments, points to the clutch circuit or a low refrigerant charge.
step: With the engine running, the AC on max and the blower on high, watch whether the compressor clutch plate pulls in and spins with the pulley
results: The clutch pulls in and stays engaged, spinning with the pulley.
Compressor plate engages and doesn't cycle.

title: AC operating pressure check
text: Applies to all models. Connect a manifold gauge set to the service ports. With the engine at 1,500 rpm, the AC at maximum and doors open, compare readings with the chart for the ambient temperature. At about 80 deg F, typical readings are 25-45 psi on the low side and 150-250 psi on the high side.
step: Connect a manifold gauge set and, with the engine at 1,500 rpm and the AC on max, compare low-side and high-side pressures with the chart for the ambient temperature
results: Low side was 38 and high side 210 at about 85 degrees out.
Gauges read right in the normal range for the outside temperature.

title: Condenser fan operation with AC on
text: Applies to all models with an electric condenser fan. With the engine idling and the AC switched on, confirm the condenser fan runs. Without airflow across the condenser at idle, high-side pressure rises and vent air warms up in traffic.
step: With the engine idling and the AC on, confirm the condenser fan is running
results: The condenser fan comes on as soon as the AC is on.
Fan runs the whole time the AC is on.

title: Automatic transmission fluid level and condition
text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission (not CVT or manual). With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.
step: With the transmission at operating temperature and the engine idling in park on level ground, check the fluid level against the hot range and look at its color and smell
results: Fluid is at the hot full mark, red, with no burnt smell.
Level is right in the hot range and the fluid looks clean.

title: Line pressure test
text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission (not CVT or manual). Connect a pressure gauge to the line pressure test port. With the engine idling in drive and the brake applied, line pressure should be 55-75 psi and rise with throttle. High line pressure produces harsh engagement; low pressure produces slipping and delayed shifts.
step: Connect a gauge to the line pressure port and read line pressure at idle in drive with the brake applied; it should be 55-75 psi
results: Line pressure was 62 at idle in drive and rose normally.
Gauge read about 65 psi at idle in gear.

title: Engine and transmission mount check
text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission (not CVT or manual). With the hood open, the brake held firmly and the engine idling, have a helper shift between drive and reverse while you watch the engine. Lift of more than about 0.5 in, or a visible gap at a mount, indicates a broken mount that can make normal shifts feel harsh.
step: With the brake held firmly, have a helper shift between drive and reverse while you watch the engine for lift or a gap at any mount
results: The engine barely moves when shifting and the mounts look intact.
No real lift at all going between drive and reverse.
